baer-heitev/1:_: Non-Jew. It appears to me that one who has a partnership with a non-Jew in chametz over which Passover passed — even though half belongs to a Jew and is forbidden in benefit — nevertheless when he divides after Pesach with the non-Jew, the non-Jew's share (since after Pesach it is only d'rabbanan we say there is clarification) is permitted in benefit. For eating requires study (Kaf HaChayyim, see there). A convert who died and left chametz over which Passover passed — whoever precedes after Passover and acquires it (for when he died it became ownerless and no one acquired it to violate) — it is permitted to him (Kaf HaChayyim, see there).
baer-heitev/2:ג: Last. For emphasis it states last yom tov (on other days he violates d'oraisa). If on last yom tov — no need for covering vessel or ten-handbreadth partition, for they did not fear he might eat in the brief time; but during Pesach need covering or partition as siman 440. It appears likewise if a gentile forgot his chametz with a Jew — same as gift here (Kaf HaChayyim).
baer-heitev/3:ג: And give it to him. If the gentile does not want to return the chametz after Pesach — forbidden to sue in their courts; forbidden for a Jew to buy from him after Pesach, and if he bought must resell to original owners (Mishna Berurah siman 43; see Magen Avraham; see Yad Aharon). Reuven and a gentile were partners and both sold chametz together to Shimon before Pesach and received money but Shimon had not yet pulled chametz from partners' domain and Passover passed — Shimon must burn it (Bnei Yaakov siman 3; see Netivot Shalom 163; Kaf HaChayyim s.k. 14; Pri Chadash).
baer-heitev/2:א: Non-Jew. Beit Yosef wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 332: I was asked about a Jew who had grain in a non-Jew's mill to grind, and the grain remained in the mill until chol hamoed of Pesach; when the seventh day of Pesach arrived the non-Jew went and ground the Jew's grain and made bread from the flour and baked the bread and brought the bread to the Jew immediately after Pesach — I answered that it is permitted to take the money for that bread from the non-Jew, and that non-Jew may eat it or sell it to a non-Jew (end of his words); and Kaf HaChayyim agreed and wrote that in siman 449 I wrote that a doubt of chametz over which Passover passed may be permitted even in eating, and if so here too it is at least a doubt lest the non-Jew exchanged. For this reason one may also be lenient if a non-Jew stole chametz outright.
baer-heitev/2:ה: That he should say. Then even if the non-Jew left it in a Jew's house on the first yom tov it is permitted; nevertheless if he did not say so it is permitted by law even if it was in his guarded courtyard — he does not acquire for him against his will, for he does not want the prohibition to be acquired. And if he reveals his mind that he wants it, acquisition applies (see 446 seif 3). It appears to me all this is regarding a gift and the like where there is no liability on the Jew; but if the non-Jew brings to a Jew's house to sell or to deposit with him, then the Jew must explicitly say he does not want to accept it so as not to become liable for it — for even if he is not liable by law but knows the non-Jew is violent and will compel payment, it is forbidden, as written above siman 440 (Kaf HaChayyim).
baer-heitev/3:ב: Outside. The way of the matter is stated — likewise even a non-Jew residing in the courtyard, even if he is his servant (Taz). This is when he has no Canaanite slave (Kaf HaChayyim); and likewise in responsum Sha'agat Aryeh siman 3 that one may not sell chametz to a maidservant acquired by a Jew. Bach wrote: in a place of trouble one may permit selling to a non-Jew all chametz in the room, even the room itself (see Choshen Mishpat siman 196 and R' Yehuda); and he must tell him even though I did not write you a deed for this sale I transfer it to you with money alone; and he must give him the key. With this, b'dieved there is no prohibition since by their law the buyer can hold it even without a key (Kaf HaChayyim). Also beware not to leave any seal on the room or on the chametz so the non-Jew cannot enter there.
baer-heitev/3:ה: Sale. It is permitted to tell him: Here is this chametz for you, and give me chametz after Pesach in return — so wrote the Gaon Maharash (end of his words). Forbidden to sell his chametz to an apostate, for though he sinned he is a Jew. If he sold, Taz wrote b'dieved one may tell the apostate to exchange it with another non-Jew or sell to a non-Jew, and the money is permitted to the Jew. There was an incident with one who held a deposit in a village — he sold his deposit to an apostate for a large sum and it was hard to lose the deposit and it was close that the Jew would not comply; I said he should exchange the deposit with another non-Jew and take another deposit from him, and then it is permitted to this Jew (Taz; see responsum Kaf HaChayyim siman 41). And for this reason one should prevent not buying on credit rent or deposit from a non-Jew immediately after Pesach.
baer-heitev/3:ו: On condition. Because of the stringency of chametz (Magen Avraham, Kaf HaChayyim).
baer-heitev/4:ב: On condition. It appears the meaning is on condition that he return it after Pesach — for then it is neither sale nor gift; but if he said on condition that he hold it for himself and do with it as he wishes, only not sell to anyone else — this is an absolute sale (Taz, end of his words).
baer-heitev/5:_: That he nullified. Even though he did not violate from the Torah, nevertheless we fear he will deceive and say he nullified though he did not, since he acted not as required — not burning chametz or selling to a non-Jew. Even absolute hefker — the law is so; even if there are witnesses that he declared hefker and nullified, it does not help if he left chametz in his house in his domain knowingly all the days of Pesach — certainly in such a case nullification or hefker does not help; but whenever he did not know of it all the days of Pesach and there are witnesses that he nullified or declared hefker, or there is absolute coercion in the sale matter and all Pesach he thought he sold and after Pesach it became known he did not sell because he was coerced — so great coercion that he said he nullified though there are no witnesses — we do not suspect evasion.
mishnah-berurah/1:ב: (2) Of a Jew — and likewise of hefker, since no prohibition was imposed by its remaining, the Sages did not forbid eating it; therefore a convert who died before Pesach and left chametz — whoever precedes and acquires after Pesach, the chametz is permitted even for eating. A Jew who has partnership with a non-Jew in chametz over which Passover passed — when he divides with the non-Jew after Passover, the non-Jew's share after Passover is permitted in benefit, for in d'rabbanan we say there is clarification and it was clarified retroactively that it belongs to a non-Jew (see Mekor Chayyim who leans specifically when the chametz stood in a non-Jew's house — and if in a Jew's house it depends on a dispute, see there); and it is possible that even for eating it is permitted (see there). The Jew's share is forbidden in benefit; and likewise two Jews who have.
mishnah-berurah/3:א: (7) Forbidden in benefit — for the Sages penalized him since he violated bal yera'eh and bal yimatzei (Gemara).
mishnah-berurah/3:ג: (9) Or under duress — meaning he knew but was under duress and could not burn it; and even though in this he did not violate, nevertheless we penalize the permitted because of the forbidden lest he leave it l'chatchila and violate — see Biur Halacha. Beit Hillel wrote in Yoreh De'ah siman 332: I was asked about a Jew who before Pesach had grain in a non-Jew's mill, and the grain remained until chol hamoed; on the seventh day the non-Jew ground it, made bread, baked, and brought the bread immediately after Pesach — I answered it is permitted to take the money from the non-Jew, and that non-Jew may eat or sell to a non-Jew (end of his words); and Chak Yakov agreed.
mishnah-berurah/3:ו: (12) Outside the house — Acharonim wrote there is no concern whether the non-Jew himself lives in the Jew's house or not; the main concern is that the non-Jew take the chametz out of the Jew's house; but the non-Jew himself, even if he is the Jew's servant and lives in his house, we are not concerned (unless he is acquired forever, for then his hand is like his master's hand and selling does not help to remove from domain). What they required here to remove from domain even though already sold and it is a mere deposit without liability — generally we do not require this except a mere partition, as above siman 440; Kaf HaChayyim wrote the law is likewise here and they did not require removal except so the non-Jew acquires by pulling.
mishnah-berurah/3:ח: (14) Provided he gives, etc. — even through his agent or wife he can transfer chametz to a non-Jew, but not through a non-Jew, for there is no agency for a non-Jew and his sale is nothing. Likewise he cannot transfer to a non-Jew's agent, for the Torah detailed agency only for Jews; even if the agent is also a non-Jew — no agency for a non-Jew, whether from non-Jew to Jew or non-Jew to non-Jew (see Biur Halacha what some poskim wrote).
mishnah-berurah/3:י: (16) Without any condition — lest the non-Jew violate the condition and the gift be void retroactively and he violate bal yera'eh, as below seif 4.
mishnah-berurah/3:כ: (17) Or that he sell — and by which acquisitions does a non-Jew acquire? There are opinions among poskim: some say his acquisition is specifically by money; some say a non-Jew acquires only by pulling to his domain or lifting something liftable; some wrote further that other acquisitions apply to a non-Jew, such as acquisition of movable property through land, acquisition of courtyard, and kinyan chalipin (sudar) — but one must be careful that the sudar belong to the non-Jew and not suffice to give their sudar at acquisition like with Jews, for that is only from the reason of zechiah which we do not apply to a non-Jew; some doubt these acquisitions and say we find them only in.
mishnah-berurah/3:ל: (18) Absolute sale — if a Jew leaves his chametz in a room of a friend who sells his chametz, he must inform the selling Jew and make him an agent to sell; if he left without knowledge, forbidden after Pesach since the Jew did not know to transfer and the non-Jew did not know to acquire (Acharonim). Further, one may tell a non-Jew: Here is chametz for you, and give me other chametz after Pesach.
mishnah-berurah/3:ס: (21) Does not work — even though throughout the Torah a gift on condition to return is a gift if the condition is fulfilled, here the Sages required an absolute gift because of chametz stringency. B'dieved if the condition was fulfilled that he returned — Acharonim dispute; see Biur Halacha. Where he said: I give you and you return it to me — see Biur Halacha.
mishnah-berurah/4:ג: (24) On condition — when he said in language of "if" — if you do such-and-such during or after Pesach the chametz is given or sold to you; as long as the condition is not fulfilled the chametz is not sold or given, and therefore he violates bal yera'eh. But if he said: I give you from now on condition that you do such-and-such, the chametz belongs to the non-Jew immediately if the condition is fulfilled later, and forbidden only because of chametz stringency, as below end of seif 3. Alternatively, even with "from now" the condition was that when he brings money he returns it — with this condition sale and gift do not take effect at all, since every hour the Jew can redeem it, as explained in Choshen Mishpat siman 207 seif 6. Know further that they agreed.
mishnah-berurah/6:ג: (28) Of hefker — for he has benefit in fulfilling his will to feed the animal; see Beit Yosef — even with found chametz not his own, forbidden to throw before a dog.
magen-avraham/3:ב: Outside the house. Meaning he must also take the chametz outside the house — for if it remains in his house it appears he accepts the non-Jew's chametz as a deposit; but by law it is permitted since the Jew is not liable; but if when the chametz is lost the Jew must return the sale price to the non-Jew, it is forbidden. If he has much chametz and cannot take it outside, he may sell him the room too; but since we hold a non-Jew does not acquire land by money alone without a deed, he should stipulate at the start of the transaction that he transfers with money alone, as in Choshen Mishpat siman 194 and 207; and he must give the key so he can enter, otherwise it is mere evasion (Bach). See siman 449 seif 5; see Shelah. Mishna Berurah siman 59 wrote he must transfer with.
magen-avraham/3:ג: Does not work. Even though elsewhere it is a gift as in first chapter of Kiddushin and Sukkah chapter 3 — because of chametz stringency it does not work, and it is an extra stringency and they did not add to compare it to another matter (Terumat HaDeshen and Hagahot Maimoniyot chapter 6 of Shabbat). Radbaz part 1 siman 140 wrote the reason: as long as the condition is pending it is like a deposit; if the condition is fulfilled, even though retroactively the chametz was the non-Jew's, before fulfillment the Jew already violated and fulfillment of the condition cannot cancel the violation already committed (Knesset HaGedolah). I would say unlike siman 441 with a non-Jew who lent on his chametz and said if I do not pay by Rosh Chodesh Nisan it is yours from now — permitted, for there one can say as above that since he will certainly pay.
magen-avraham/4:ב: He thereby violates bal yera'eh. One who deposits chametz with a non-Jew violates, as siman 440 (Mishna Berurah). It must deal when the Jew himself attached the condition, e.g. that if the Jew has money he will return it — in such a case it is not a sale at all, as Choshen Mishpat siman 207 (end of his words), and worse than a pledge where he said if I do not redeem before Rosh Chodesh Nisan it is yours from now; but here redemption is always in his power. Alternatively, the Jew attached the sale to a condition, e.g. if you do such-and-such the chametz is yours — as long as the condition is not fulfilled it is not his sale; but if he said: I give you from now on condition to return or on condition you do such-and-such, this is an absolute sale.
magen-avraham/5:_: Even though he nullified. Even though he did not violate from the Torah, we fear he will deceive and say he nullified though he did not (Tur); and see siman 447; likewise one who declares chametz hefker — so Rosh and poskim in the name of Yerushalmi, unlike one opinion (end of his words). R' Shimon HaLevi siman 12 wrote: one on a ship wanted to permit declaring all his chametz hefker and re-acquire after Pesach and sell — but not to eat, for this is uncommon and because of chametz stringency I was not comfortable to act (Knesset HaGedolah). It is obvious that even if the chametz is not with him he can sell to a non-Jew by one of the acquisitions mentioned, and then the non-Jew acquired the chametz wherever it is; see above siman 426 seif 3.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ג: But with a deed — meaning requires both: money and also deed; no concern whether money first or deed first — so there in Choshen Mishpat; Shelah wrote even if the deed is written in our script, i.e. Hebrew — he writes to the gentile: I sell room such-and-such with all inside (end of his words); what he wrote with all, etc. — see below.
machatzit-hashekel/2:א: (s.k. 2) He should not show — for from the default we say he does not want a prohibition to be acquired, as we say in Bava Metzia chapter Sho'el; rather it is better if he explicitly says he does not want [the non-Jew] to acquire it in his domain.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ב: And if he has much chametz, etc. — it implies specifically when he cannot take it out it is permitted; but if he can take it from the house he must take it out; likewise in Sefer Ateret Rosh — so is custom in Prague that beer sellers must take all chametz from their houses; they asked why they differ from wine sellers who may keep chametz in the house and sell to a gentile. He answered: beer sellers differ for they cannot take out the chametz (end of his words).
machatzit-hashekel/4:ד: And behold, etc. with money alone — and Shelah concluded on this; nevertheless one must inform the gentile and explain well so his mind relies on the leniency (end of his words).
machatzit-hashekel/4:ה: Bach. In truth here Bach wrote it suffices if he gifts that he acquire with money alone; but in Choshen Mishpat he brought Shach in the name of Bach who disagrees on this law and holds that stipulating to acquire with bare money does not work; it is possible Bach is lenient regarding chametz since otherwise it is not in his domain but Scripture made it as if in his domain, as Magen Avraham wrote afterward.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ו: And siman 449 seif 5 — meaning Bach wrote that though one can rent the room to a gentile and land-rental is acquired by a gentile through money alone, it is not possible for two reasons: one, we hold rental does not acquire; and further Yerushalmi forbids renting a room to gentiles to use chametz — and Pri Chadash rejected these reasons: what they said rental does not acquire — nevertheless for chametz it helps, as Pesachim daf 4 teaches chametz is different because it is written lo yimatze; also through rental it is not in his possession. What Yerushalmi forbids — we do not hold like that Yerushalmi; nevertheless for the law he agreed with Bach that there is no remedy through rental, for it is profiting from benefit prohibitions which is forbidden; and for this reason he wrote in siman 449 seif 5 in Magen Avraham s.k. 16.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ח: And Mishna Berurah, etc. with money and pulling, etc. — for regarding this gold R' Yehuda and R' Levi dispute: R' Yehuda holds d'oraisa money acquires for a Jew, and Scripture wrote "when you sell to your fellow" and excludes a gentile — if so for a gentile money does not work except pulling is required; R' Levi holds d'oraisa for a Jew pulling acquires — if so for a gentile the opposite: specifically money acquires and not pulling. Rashi and those of his school ruled like R' Levi; Rabbenu Tam and those of his school ruled like R' Yehuda. To satisfy both, Beit Yosef siman 317 wrote regarding annulling firstborn sanctity to transfer the mother while pregnant to a gentile and a gentile animal is exempt from firstborn — for this acquisition he required both money and pulling, or acquisition of the place where the animal stands.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ט: But most poskim hold like Rashi — as Acharonim wrote, on the contrary most poskim hold like Rabbenu Tam; nevertheless for the law it helps b'dieved. Money alone — for Mishna Berurah wrote pulling alone also helps b'dieved; even though in his view most hold a gentile specifically needs money — if so for us the opposite helps b'dieved, money alone, even though most hold like Rabbenu Tam that a gentile needs pulling. With revealed intent it suffices, as Beit Yosef siman 431 wrote — therefore nullification from Torah of hefker works; and per many poskim even nullification in the heart alone works, though for hefker such does not work since he did not say language of hefker but to nullify to be like dust (some also require hefker before three), as written in.
machatzit-hashekel/4:י: And requires study — in Yerushalmi regarding acquisitions, place of confusion — Kaf HaChayyim wrote in the name of responsum Avnei Nezer: the intent is not that by transferring place it becomes the gentile's courtyard and the courtyard acquires the chametz, for courtyard is from the reason of agency and there is no agency for a gentile; rather the intent is through agav movable property is acquired with land (and therefore the language should be agav and not "with," as Choshen Mishpat siman 210 per one opinion there). However in responsum Avodat HaGershuni siman 120 he wrote — therefore Tur Yoreh De'ah siman 317 wrote regarding annulling firstborn sanctity that the clear acquisition is that he acquires the place and gave in that responsum a reason why this acquisition is clear, that through pulling.
machatzit-hashekel/4:כ: And I already wrote it is difficult to transfer to a gentile through agav, for a gentile's mind does not rely on acquiring through agav; and where his mind is not to acquire through this acquisition he did not acquire, as written in the name of responsum Avnei Nezer in the name of poskim. Therefore it occurred to me better to sell to a gentile woman who has no husband — for in such a case he concedes to responsum Avnei Nezer that her courtyard acquires for her, as explained in Choshen Mishpat siman 243 that a minor has no courtyard — for a man, courtyard is from agency and there is no agency for a minor; but a minor girl has a courtyard, for regarding a woman courtyard is from the reason of "hand," and a minor girl has a hand. If so a gentile woman — one can say "hand," and even though a woman's courtyard from "hand" we learn from divorce as in first chapter of Bava Metzia, and divorce does not exist for a gentile — nevertheless one can say.
machatzit-hashekel/4:ל: And so merchants practice, etc. — meaning Jewish merchants; and this is the law of situmta explained in Choshen Mishpat siman 210; but Shach wrote in the name of Bach that for land situmta does not acquire unless it is known clearly that the custom in that place is to acquire land through situmta; all the more acquisition between gentile and Jew which in their law is obvious. Also he gave partial payment — in responsum Avnei Nezer siman 102 he wrote: furthermore tell him that even in their law they would not rule so except in an absolute sale; but in our case he sold two cows for half a pig — possible that even in their law he does not acquire though Tosafot Avodah Zarah chapter 2 daf 71 wrote — nevertheless the gentile need not give money worth, etc.; rather it suffices that he acquire with a perutah (end of his words).
machatzit-hashekel/4:נ: And likewise in Yoreh De'ah siman 317, etc. — since poskim needed to find a remedy to sell the animal to annul firstborn sanctity through money and pulling or acquisition of place as above — all the more they should fix easily to acquire through an acquisition that works in their law. From this Shach siman 123 brings proof not like Rabbenu Tam who holds chalipin works for a gentile — for then poskim should have given this remedy for chametz and firstborn to acquire through chalipin; or they hold chalipin does not work for a gentile (end of his words). As we say with a gentile's knowledge it is ownerless — these are the words of the Gemara Bava Kamma daf 117a: Rav Safra was traveling in a caravan and joined them; a lion came to guard their animals from beasts and thieves, and they gave him each night one donkey to eat. When Rav Safra's time came.
machatzit-hashekel/5:א: (s.k. 5) Does not work, etc. Radbaz, etc. — meaning Radbaz's words can be explained two ways: either because all Pesach days the condition is pending and unclear that it belongs to the gentile, and since it is doubtful the Jew violates; or because it is in the gentile's hand not to fulfill the condition, and a matter in his hand to do or not fulfill is as if done and the gentile did not fulfill the condition and it is certainly the Jew's. At first Magen Avraham explained Radbaz's intent from the second reason; therefore he wrote: I would say unlike siman 441, even though there too one can say since it is in the Jew's hand to redeem.
machatzit-hashekel/5:ב: And likewise regarding challah in the Gemara daf 40 and below siman 457 seif 2 — one who separates challah from impure dough on Pesach yom tov may not call it challah until baked, for if he calls it challah while still dough it is forbidden to bake, for it is not fit for any person since it is impure; if he leaves the challah so and does not bake it, it will leaven; and even though it is not the Jew's and will not reach a kohen, we say the Jew violates since if he wishes he can ask a sage about vows and annul vows and it returns to being fit — therefore even if he did not ask, he violates because it is in his power to ask, unlike there where it is in the Jew's hand to ask about his vow and it is like his own.
machatzit-hashekel/5:ג: But here if the gentile wishes, etc. — meaning here the matter is not in the Jew's hand to fulfill or not fulfill the condition but in the gentile's hand; therefore it need not be the Jew's since the matter is not in his hand.
machatzit-hashekel/5:ד: And what he wrote that all this when the condition is pending, etc. — now he comes to reject: do not say even without "since" he violates because the matter was doubtful all Pesach days as above.
machatzit-hashekel/5:ו: Therefore for chametz — if he says and you return it to me after Pesach it works, for he intended a gift all Pesach days; and even stam if he said and you return it to me, we are witnesses his intent is to return specifically after Pesach. Also per Taz there who distinguishes: when he says and you return it to me it does not imply a condition but return and return from the first giving; for chametz with revealed intent it suffices — we are witnesses he did not intend return but an absolute gift, only he asks him to return afterward, as Magen Avraham wrote. After investigation I found something similar in Sefer Ateret Rosh.
machatzit-hashekel/7:א: (s.k. 7) He thereby violates, etc. — if the Jew will have money, etc. — meaning he did not set a time for this, but whenever the Jew gives money the gentile must return the chametz — if so no hour is clarified that it belongs to the gentile even one hour, and therefore it is not a sale; similarly Semag wrote in siman 207 s.k. 11 (end of his words).
machatzit-hashekel/7:ב: Alternatively the Jew attached the sale to a condition — meaning he did not say from now but the sale takes effect only at the time the condition is fulfilled; but if he said: Here it is for you from now, etc. — and even though Magen Avraham wrote above siman 441 s.k. 2 that even from now does not work except for a loan and pledge (see there the reason) and not for a gift — that is for us who hold in Choshen Mishpat that from now does not remove asmakhta and there is a dispute in Darkei Chaim (see there siman 207 seif 9 and Semag s.k. 44); but Rambam holds from now alone even for a gift removes asmakhta, as explained there in Choshen Mishpat. Here Shulchan Aruch wrote "he thereby violates" in Rambam's language; and Magen Avraham here brought Maggid Mishneh explaining Rambam's words — if so what Magen Avraham wrote here.
turei-zahav/4:_: To a non-Jew outside the house. Bach, Beit Yosef — it implies from Terumat HaDeshen's words that giving chametz to a non-Jew does not work (unless he is a non-Jew) outside the house; the intent is not that the non-Jew be a stranger not living in a Jew's house, but regarding the chametz — if it is in a Jew's house there is no concern; this certainly has no taste or smell, and further it is worse than chametz in his house; and further Terumat HaDeshen did not write outside the house but outside his house — implying he spoke of the chametz being outside the house, and we are not concerned about the non-Jew even if in the Jew's servant's house, for below he permits even one who recognizes him and is accustomed, etc. All this I wrote per Beit Yosef in the name of Terumat HaDeshen; but the essence of the matter we do not lean — for it is explicit in first chapter of Bava Metzia that I brought in siman 440.
turei-zahav/6:_: And he may not give on condition. It appears the meaning is on condition that he return it after Pesach — for then it is neither sale nor gift; but if he said on condition that he hold it for himself and do as he wishes, only not sell to anyone else — this is an absolute sale even all year; it appears anyone may say so explicitly to the non-Jew and it helps that no one can buy that chametz from the non-Jew because he sold on this condition, and the sale returns to the non-Jew and the Jew owner can buy it back; but then the owner is forbidden to sue the Jew who bought from the non-Jew and say give me the chametz at that sale price, for thereby he reveals his mind that the sale was void and the chametz returns to.
baer-heitev/2:ב: Doron. If a gentile gave or sold wheat etc. to a Jew and he accepted, and after Pesach it became known there was chametz inside — l'chatchila it appears the chametz is permitted after Pesach as gentile's chametz; proof from Nedarim 35: the recipient can say I wanted leniency not prohibition — Rashi, Ran, Rosh; unlike one who takes hekdesh money unintentionally. But what another gave him.
baer-heitev/3:ד: Finished. One may give through his brother or wife; he need not tell his wife to return later. Incident: one had chametz and wanted to sell to a gentile; he schemed not to mention his chametz but left it in a friend's room knowing the friend would sell that room with chametz inside to the gentile and gave the key; the friend sold the room and the hidden chametz was sold with it without the selling Jew or buying gentile knowing — forbidden (Chinuch Beit Yehuda siman 13).
mishnah-berurah/5:_: (25) Forbidden even though he nullified — or declared hefker; forbidden even in benefit. Even when nullified he does not violate bal yera'eh, nevertheless Sages feared if we permit when nullified, everyone will leave chametz until after Pesach claiming hefker before Pesach. Know many Acharonim wrote even if he checked per our custom and found chametz after Pesach — forbidden in benefit; some lenient when checked, nullified, then found — he did all required; their view: at least for benefit do not forbid; in great loss rely on them (see Biur Halacha seif 3 s.v. even). One on a ship or road with chametz and no gentile to sell — declared hefker before witnesses whether he may acquire and benefit after Pesach — Acharonim dispute, majority forbid; in great loss permit selling to gentile or exchanging. If on road remembered chametz at home, no one to sell on eve — declared hefker before witnesses — may rely on lenient view to re-acquire after Pesach, since not in his hand and could not sell or burn as required.
mishnah-berurah/1:א: (1) Chametz, etc. — meaning whether dough or even bread in a place where they practice leniency with gentile bread.
mishnah-berurah/2:ג: (5) He should not show, etc. — if it would be apparent he desires it, such as telling him place it in a certain hidden spot in my courtyard — his courtyard acquires for him; but if not apparent, even if the gentile leaves it as a gift in his house it is permitted, for presumably he does not want a prohibition to be acquired and his courtyard does not acquire against his will; therefore even if this were on the first yom tov it is permitted.
mishnah-berurah/3:ה: (11) To a gentile — and to a Jewish apostate forbidden to sell, for his law is like a Jew in every matter, and he further violates lifnei iver; the chametz is forbidden after Pesach in benefit. B'dieved if he sold to a Jewish apostate for a small amount because he knows him and knows he will return after Pesach — since he erred thinking an apostate's law is like a gentile — one may permit in great loss: tell the apostate to exchange the chametz with a gentile for other chametz or sell it, and the exchange or money is permitted, as explained end of siman 443.
mishnah-berurah/3:ז: (13) And he will return and give it to him — if the gentile does not want to return it, forbidden to sue him in their courts or compel him otherwise; if he gave only partial payment and the rest is a loan he refuses to pay — certainly permitted to sue in their law for payment or chametz as payment of debt. Acharonim wrote: another Jew may not buy the chametz from the gentile after Pesach; if he bought he must return to original owners; if he overpaid the gentile improperly, he need return only proper amount.
mishnah-berurah/3:מ: (19) For a small amount — one need not fear void sale, for he knows himself it is worth more and agrees to transfer so it not remain in his domain forbidden in benefit. Better he sell to his buyers, for then presumably the gentile will return after Pesach (see Biur Halacha on our custom today). Acharonim wrote: though l'chatchila one should sell with money and pulling, if chametz is abundant and impossible to pull all, or chametz is elsewhere the gentile cannot pull — he may transfer by other acquisitions such as marking practiced in some places, hand-clap (tschlak), perutah where custom completes sale, or key transfer where custom (but at least say I sell you such-and-such chametz for such sum, not merely I sell the key). Or sell through agav — sell or rent land/room and say acquire my chametz there; agav acquires even not piled; land acquired with money and deed, rental with money alone; partial gold (auf gab) suffices with loan for rest. If house not his but rented, sale does not help — rent room stam for vessels without saying for chametz (see siman 449). Jew bought from gentile, paid, did not pull — l'chatchila sell before Pesach; if not sold and Passover passed, permitted per majority who need pulling; if pulled without money, some forbid; if local custom buys with money, Pri Megadim leans stringent (see Shaarei Teshuvah s.k. 9).
